Flight Price Prediction · Exploratory Data Analysis

Training records: 15,589 · Holdout records: 3,898 · Target: price · No test-target training

Key findings & modeling decisions

  • Only train.csv contains labels. Never fit on test.csv labels, pseudo-label test observations, or select models using Kaggle public leaderboard alone.
  • ID restarts at 1 in both files. Treat ID only as an output key; it is not a meaningful explanatory feature.
  • Flight-code prefix exactly identifies observed airline names when airline is not missing. Impute airline from this per-fold mapping; avoid treating missingness as a random category without testing.
  • Duration and airline are each missing in ~20% of observations. Test feature-missing indicators; impute duration within route/stops if robust, and compare with tree models that allow NaN.
  • Duplicate input feature combinations sometimes have different prices; not all residual error is removable from available predictors.
  • Many ticket classes/routes show different price dynamics. Try a global model with interactions and separate Economy/Business experts.
  • Consider a group-based flight-ID holdout as a stress test, alongside ordinary randomized K-fold; unseen flight codes appear in the test set.
  • Do not clip high prices simply for being outliers: business-class high fares are legitimate for this target.
  • RMSE, MAE and R² are reported pending official competition scoring metric. RMSE penalizes missing expensive fares sharply.
  • CatBoost/LightGBM/XGBoost are gradient-boosted decision-tree models, not neural networks.

Coverage diagnostics: 3,089 of 3,089 missing training airlines can be reconstructed from observed flight prefixes; 35/3,898 test rows (0.90%) contain a flight identifier not present in training. Submission IDs match the test IDs: True.

Visual EDA · univariate, bivariate and multivariate

Target price: raw distribution

The raw price distribution is right-skewed and contains expensive business-class flights; removing these indiscriminately would be unsafe.

Target price: log(1 + price)

A log transformation compresses the high-price tail, but using it for training depends on the Kaggle metric.

Flight class: frequency

Class balance matters for validation: stratify folds so both Economy and Business are represented consistently.

Class-conditional price distribution

Prices differ dramatically between classes; consider class interactions or specialist models.

Univariate distribution: airline

Assess frequency imbalance and rare categories in airline; rare levels must be handled safely in validation.

Price vs duration: class-colored scatter

Flight class mediates the relation; fit conditional patterns rather than relying on global correlations.

Price vs days_left: class-colored scatter

Flight class mediates the relation; fit conditional patterns rather than relying on global correlations.

Days until departure vs median price, separated by class

Investigate nonlinear and interacting lead-time relationships; tree ensembles can capture non-monotonicity.

Median price by duration bucket and class

Duration effects may vary by class and are conditional on route/stops.

Departure × arrival time: median price

Time interactions can matter more than individual main effects, although class/route confounding needs consideration.

Economy: route median price matrix

The route can explain pricing differences inside Economy even after flight class is controlled.

Business: route median price matrix

The route can explain pricing differences inside Business even after flight class is controlled.

Origin–destination frequency matrix

Small and empty routes can be hard to predict; include route and component city features.

Stops × flight class vs price

Stop counts affect fares differently within classes; beware extremely rare multi-stop records.

Target by missingness pattern and class

Evaluate whether missingness indicators carry target signal within each ticket class.

Numeric + ordinal Spearman correlation matrix

Class is likely dominant in unconditional correlation; conditional effects and nonlinear patterns require multivariate models.

Train/test categorical shift (JS distance)

Compare train and test feature distributions without using test labels; drift can weaken a good CV result.

Univariate mutual information ranking (descriptive only)

Mutual information can detect nonlinear associations but is univariate and sensitive to high-cardinality features. It is not a validated feature-selection score.

Reproducible from eda.py; all price statistics use train.csv only. Categorical and numeric shift uses test.csv features only. Diagnostic MI is exploratory, not cross-validated selection.
